title: Law from verses
hook: Mekhilta, Sifra and Sifre read legal meaning out of the Torah's words

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Yerushalmi, and your line: two talmuds. Did you find a second version of something? Both Talmuds grow from the Mishnah. Today, books that grow straight from the verses. Day one thousand one hundred four.

Here's a question the Torah seems to answer in two directions at once. It commands the Sabbath with real force: keep it, don't work, it's holy. And it also cares, over and over, about keeping people alive. So what happens on a Sabbath when someone is in danger and the help they need is work? Rush to them, or rest? A rule book might simply list an exception. The sages wanted more than an exception. They wanted to show where in the Torah's own words the answer was already sitting. So they went back to a single verse and read it very, very slowly. Today's word is the name for that kind of reading.
screen: `KEEP THE SABBATH.` → `KEEP PEOPLE ALIVE.` → `WHICH COMES FIRST?`

segments.voice: Law from verses. It's a way of reading where the sages draw practical law out of the Torah's exact words, and a family of books preserves it. Start with the books. The Mekhilta reads the book of Exodus. The Sifra reads Leviticus. The Sifre reads Numbers and Deuteronomy. Each walks through long stretches of its Torah book, verse after verse, asking what each word teaches about how to live. Second, how they work. The Mishnah, you remember, often states a law plainly, with no verse attached. These books do the opposite. They quote a verse, press on one word, and say: from here we learn. Third, the Sabbath question. In Exodus the Torah says of the Sabbath, in the JPS translation, "for it is holy unto you." Unto you. A teaching preserved in the Mekhilta, and in the Talmud too, leans on that small phrase: the Sabbath is handed over to you, and you are not handed over to the Sabbath. So when a life is in danger, the Sabbath gives way. The answer was sitting in one small phrase the whole time; it took a slow reader to find it. Fourth, why it matters. These books show the sages' work in the open. You can see the verse, the word they pressed, and the law that came out. Not every reader agrees with every reading, and the books themselves record disagreements. But the claim they make is quiet and large: the law isn't stacked on top of the Torah. It grows from inside it, word by word. Law from verses.
screen: `MEKHILTA, SIFRA, SIFRE.` · `QUOTE A VERSE, PRESS ONE WORD.` · `HOLY UNTO YOU.` · `THE LAW GROWS FROM INSIDE.` · then, large: `LAW FROM VERSES.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is reading one midrash, slowly, the way the sages did. Take the phrase from today: for it is holy unto you. Settle, and breathe. Say the phrase once in your head. Then lean on one word at a time. Holy. What does it change, for something to be holy? Unto. A gift moving toward someone. You. Not the Sabbath's servant, but the one it was given to. Don't hurry to a conclusion. Let each word have its own breath. The bell holds the time.
Law from verses. The way the sages, in books like the Mekhilta, Sifra and Sifre, draw practical law out of the Torah's exact words. Today's word.
Your line: law from verses. Today, take one rule you follow, at home or at work, and ask where it came from. Find the sentence it grew out of, if there is one. Day one thousand one hundred four.

howItsDone: Students study the Mekhilta, Sifra and Sifre alongside the Torah portion or the Talmud, tracing a law back to the verse and the word it was read from. Their teachings are also quoted throughout the Talmud.

original.note: Hebrew: the name for close reading of the Torah's words. Midrash that draws out law is called midrash halakha.

trapdoor: what you thought: the rabbis made up rules and called them Torah.
what it means: books like the Mekhilta, Sifra and Sifre draw law out of the Torah's exact words, verse by verse.
what a scholar hears: midrash halakha, and the reading of Exodus 31:14, 'unto you', as the basis for setting aside the Sabbath to save a life.

sources.quoted: for it is holy unto you

notes: Please confirm the JPS 1917 wording 'for it is holy unto you' in Exodus 31:14.

The teaching 'the Sabbath is handed over to you, and you are not handed over to the Sabbath' is attributed in Mekhilta Ki Tisa and Yoma 85b to Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya; the sage is not named in the script. Paraphrased; please confirm.
The Mekhilta records other derivations for saving life on the Sabbath; the script presents one and notes that the books record disagreements.
Book assignments (Mekhilta: Exodus; Sifra: Leviticus; Sifre: Numbers and Deuteronomy) follow the index; please confirm.
The word 'midrash' is not given an etymology, under the claims rule.

Editor: 'sitting in two words' changed to 'one small phrase' (the Hebrew 'unto you' is a single word, lakhem, so the count was wrong); 'walks through a Torah book verse by verse' softened to 'long stretches of its Torah book', since the Mekhilta does not cover all of Exodus. Attribution check for a Keeper: the Mekhilta gives the saying to Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, while Yoma 85b gives it to Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef; the voice names neither.
